title: Spelling Verb Endings
keyIdea: An ending is a few letters added to the end of a root word. -ing tells you something is happening now (jumping), -ed tells you it happened in the past (helped), and -s tells you it happens again and again (Sam plays). Words that end in s, x, z, sh or ch take -es instead (fixes, wishes). -er means more and -est means the most of all (taller, tallest). With these words the root is not changed at all: write the whole root, then the ending. -ed is always spelt ed, even when it sounds like t (jumped) or d (played).
familyTip: Play 'now, yesterday, every day'. Pick a doing word such as jump, kick or help. Your child says it three ways: Now I am jumping. Yesterday I jumped. Every day I jump. Then write one of them together and circle the root. If they write jumpt, say the word slowly and remind them: the past ending is always spelt e, d.

visual.caption: Is it happening now, or did it happen in the past? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: add the ending a time clue needs, spell -ed by rule, label tall, taller, tallest, and cut words to the root.

kid: A root word is the main word, like jump. We can add an ending to it. The ending tells us more.
Now I am jumping. Yesterday I jumped. Every day Sam jumps. The root jump stays the same each time.
The ed ending can sound like t, like in jumped. It can sound like d, like in played. It is still spelt e, d.
Some words end in x, s or sh. They take es, like fix and fixes. You can hear the extra beat. Add er to say more. Add est to say the most of all. tall, taller, tallest.
adult: Ages 5 to 6. English Appendix 1 for Year 1 lists adding -s and -es to words (plural nouns and the third person singular of verbs), adding -ing, -ed and -er to verbs where no change is needed to the root word (hunting, hunted, hunter; buzzing, buzzed, buzzer; jumping, jumped, jumper), and adding -er and -est to adjectives where no change is needed (grander, grandest; fresher, freshest; quicker, quickest). Common Core L.1.1e and L.1.1f cover the matching grammar: verbs for past, present and future, and frequently occurring adjectives.

The key spelling idea is that the root word is written whole and unchanged, then the suffix. The past tense -ed has three sounds, /t/ after voiceless sounds (jumped, helped), /d/ after voiced sounds (played), and /ɪd/ after t or d (wanted), but one spelling. -es is used after s, x, z, sh and ch, where it adds a syllable (fix-es). -er compares two things and -est picks out one from three or more.

Common mistakes: spelling -ed as it sounds (jumpt, playd, wantid), dropping the g from -ing (jumpin), doubling a letter that should not be doubled (jumpping), writing fixs, adding more to a word that already has -er (more taller), using -est for two things, and spelling -est as ist. Words that do change their root, such as hopping, hoping and cried, belong to the next step (Suffixes), so this lesson only uses roots that need no change.

In the lab your child drags -ing, -ed or -s onto five roots to match a time clue, picks the spelling of four -ed words from how they sound, taps towers and snakes in the order tall, taller, tallest, cuts six words back to their root, and finishes four sentences, one of which needs -es.

practice.hint: Yesterday is in the past. The past ending is spelt e, d.
practice.explain: play + ed = played. It sounds like d at the end, but it is spelt ed.

practice.prompt: A root word has {r} letters, like jump. You add -ing and change nothing else. How many letters does the new word have?
practice.hint: The root keeps all its letters. Then count i, n, g.
practice.explain: The root keeps its {r} letters and -ing adds 3, so {=r+3}. jump has 4, jumping has 7.

practice.hint: wash ends in sh. What do you add after sh?
practice.explain: After s, x, z, sh or ch you add -es, so Mum washes the dishes.

practice.prompt: A root word has {r} letters, like help. You add -ed. How many letters does the new word have?
practice.hint: No letters change. -ed adds e and d.
practice.explain: {r} letters + 2 for e and d = {=r+2}. help has 4, helped has 6.

practice.hint: Out of three, the most of all takes -est.
practice.explain: longest picks out the most of all three. It is spelt e, s, t.

pool.prompt: Which is spelt right? (it sounds like jump-t)
pool.hint: The past ending is always spelt the same way.
pool.explain: It sounds like t, but the past ending is spelt ed: jumped.

pool.prompt: What is the root word in helping?
pool.hint: Take off the ending -ing. A real word is left.
pool.explain: helping = help + ing. The root help did not change.

pool.prompt: Look! The dog is ... the ball.
pool.hint: Look! means it is happening now.
pool.explain: It is happening now, so is + kicking.

pool.prompt: Sam writes {a} words that end in -ed and {b} words that end in -ing. How many words have an ending?
pool.hint: Add the -ed words and the -ing words.
fix ends in x. Every day takes the -s or -es ending.
pool.explain: After x you add -es: he fixes the box every day.

pool.hint: Two people are compared, so which ending means more?
pool.explain: For two, use -er: taller. It already means more, so do not add more.

pool.prompt: Which is spelt right? (it sounds like want-id)
pool.hint: The past ending is still e, d, even with the extra beat.
pool.explain: want + ed = wanted. It has an extra beat, but it is spelt ed.

pool.prompt: {n} towers stand in a row. Each one is taller than the one before. How many towers are taller than the first one?
pool.hint: Every tower after the first one is taller than it.
pool.explain: All but the first are taller, so {=n-1}. The last one is the tallest.

pool.hint: Keep sing whole and write all of i, n, g.
pool.explain: sing + ing = singing. No extra g and no missing g.
quickest means the most quick of all of them.
